(out/'manuscript.txt').write_text(''.join(text))
print(''.join(text[:3]))

strengths: The proposed integration of ten facial analysis tasks addresses a useful practical problem. Sharing computation across segmentation, landmarks, pose, recognition, and demographic prediction could simplify deployment even without leading every benchmark.

The experiments cover many established benchmarks and show promising results, including 3.52 MAE on BIWI, 3.05 NME on the full 300W test set, and 91.83% attribute accuracy on CelebA. The 300VW Category-C result of 6.75 NME versus STARLoss's 8.42 provides additional evidence under challenging conditions.
Table 7 provides useful evidence for bidirectional attention: relative to standard cross-attention, head-pose MAE improves from 4.63 to 3.52 and landmark NME from 5.30 to 4.67.

Figure 2 communicates the architecture clearly, and the appendix provides dataset descriptions and augmentation details. The reported reductions in parameters, FLOPs, and latency relative to Faceptor suggest a practically relevant efficiency contribution.
weaknesses: The central claim of unified inference needs stronger validation. Appendix F.2 and F.7 use five-point alignment for landmarks and recognition, while F.3 uses loose crops for pose estimation. Section 3.4 identifies this incompatibility but does not establish a common inference preprocessing protocol that preserves all reported accuracies. The additional three training epochs 'for some tasks' also leave unclear whether every result comes from the same final checkpoint.

The claimed architectural novelty is insufficiently distinguished from prior work. Task self-attention followed by token-to-image and image-to-token attention, repeated twice with a final token-to-image attention stage, closely resembles SAM's two-way decoder. SAM [40] is cited as a foundation model, but this architectural relationship is not discussed. The manuscript should identify what is technically new beyond adapting established components to facial tasks.

Table 3 contains a consequential numerical inconsistency: the ten displayed FaceXFormer class F1 scores average to 91.01, rather than the reported 92.01. This would still exceed Faceptor's 90.89, but reduces the apparent improvement from 1.12 to 0.12 points. The aggregation or underlying values must be reconciled before the headline parsing result can be assessed confidently.

The experiments do not adequately isolate the claimed source of efficiency and multitask gains. There is no decoder-depth comparison establishing that bidirectional attention enables replacing nine layers with two, nor a controlled single-task or task-subset training comparison measuring transfer. Comparisons matching backbone and resolution would strengthen the efficiency attribution. Table 9 also needs the inference device, batch size, and preprocessing scope.

Important reproduction and evaluation details remain unresolved. Loss weights and handling of missing task annotations are unspecified. Appendix F.5 introduces MORPH-II training and evaluation, whereas the main protocol and Table 4 identify UTKFace; the associated splits are unclear. Joint training also requires explicit overlap checks across related datasets, particularly 300W-LP and 300W, to establish that landmark test imagery is excluded from other training tasks.

The ten-task claim lacks quantitative race-classification results. The substantial tradeoffs in expression recognition and face recognition also deserve clearer treatment: the reported scores trail QFace on RAF-DB and SwinFace on mean verification accuracy. These tradeoffs can be acceptable for a unified system, but the broad superiority claims exceed the demonstrated evidence.

The bias analysis is welcome, but its conclusions are overstated. Table 8 reports an age accuracy gap of 0.50 for FaceXFormer, larger than CLIP's absolute gap of 0.30 and FaRL's 0.35, contradicting the claim of the smallest discrepancy. Pooling six racial categories into one group can conceal disparities, and no ablation establishes that race co-training causes reduced bias. The proposed surveillance and automatic-annotation applications also warrant discussion of privacy and propagation of demographic labeling errors.
